## 1. Goal

Find out whether an AI reading the literature can measure one of two things
in immunology:

1. **The half-life of facts.** The time until half of the claims in an area
   are superseded or shown to be untrue.
2. **The variance in belief.** How far immunologists disagree about the same
   process or definition at one point in time.

Either number would say how much structural uncertainty a QSP model of that
area carries before any data are fit. The first test is B cell
immunophenotypes (Section 3).

**Out of scope.** Building or fitting a QSP model, and judging which B cell
definition is correct. The project measures agreement and change, not truth.

## 2. Background

**The half-life of facts.** The term is from Samuel Arbesman's book *The
Half-Life of Facts* (2012). The one published estimate in medicine that the
Google Doc cites is about 45 years for hepatitis and cirrhosis. That figure is
presumably Poynard and colleagues, "Truth survival in clinical research"
(*Annals of Internal Medicine*, 2002), in which experts reread conclusions
from papers going back decades and judged which still held. ⚠️ Not checked
against the paper.

**The 2024 survey idea.** The
[Google Doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1cC56NsD-lwQEeJK78XGLqNEyyO51PZ0MZx6NLKl2G4U/edit)
proposed a 5 to 10 minute survey of immunologists, run by a team of five or
fewer modelers and posted to Zenodo, asking which areas of immuno-oncology are
understood well enough to model. Its reasons not to do it still apply:

- Modelers who work with immunologists already accept that much of the immune
  system is poorly understood.
- A survey takes a lot of work, and its answers change with time.
- It is hard to stay motivated unless the answer is needed for one's own
  work. The doc names B cell subsets and depth of response in autoimmune
  disease as work that would need it.

**What AI changes.** Asking an AI to extract the same claim from hundreds of
papers, with the year of each, is much cheaper than a survey. It covers every
published author rather than the people who answer, and the publication year
gives the time axis that a one-off survey lacks.

## 3. Starting Point: B Cell Immunophenotypes

B cell subsets in blood are identified by flow cytometry from a few surface
markers. The markers most used are CD19 and CD20 (B cell lineage), CD27
(memory), IgD (naive and unswitched), CD38 and CD24 (transitional and
plasmablast), and CD21, CD11c, T-bet and CXCR5 (atypical subsets). The table
is a common scheme, written from memory; papers differ, and measuring how they
differ is this project. ⚠️ Not checked against a source.

| Subset | A common definition |
|---|---|
| Transitional | CD19+ CD24hi CD38hi |
| Naive | CD19+ IgD+ CD27− |
| Unswitched memory | IgD+ CD27+ |
| Switched memory | IgD− CD27+ |
| Double negative (DN) | IgD− CD27−, split into DN1 (CD21+ CD11c−), DN2 (CD21− CD11c+) and DN3 (CD21− CD11c−) |
| Atypical or age-associated B cells | CD21lo CD11c+ T-bet+, overlapping DN2 |
| Plasmablasts | CD27hi CD38hi, CD20− |

: B cell subsets and a common marker definition {tbl-colwidths="[30,70]"}

The B cell area suits a first test for three reasons:

- **The definitions are written down.** A gating strategy is a short, explicit
  list of markers, so it can be extracted and compared without judgment.
- **The definitions have moved.** The double-negative subsets and the
  atypical or age-associated B cells were named in the last 15 years, and the
  same cells carry several names.
- **The work needs it.** The [B cell reset](../imm-bcell-reset/index.qmd)
  project depends on which subsets are measured and how they are defined.

## 4. How AI Would Measure It

**Variance in belief.** For each paper reporting B cell subsets in human
blood, extract each subset's name and marker definition, with the year,
disease area and lab. Then count, for each subset name, how many distinct
definitions are in use, and for each marker combination, how many names it
goes by.

**Half-life.** Follow the same extraction across publication years. A
definition's life runs from its first appearance to the year its share of
papers drops below half its peak. Some definitions are refined rather than
dropped, such as DN splitting into DN1 to DN3, and those need their own
category.

**Checks on the AI.**

- A person checks a random sample of extractions against the papers'
  methods sections, and the error rate is reported.
- The search and extraction prompts are saved, so a second run can be
  compared with the first.

## 5. Open Questions

1. Which number to aim for first: the half-life needs many years of papers,
   and the variance needs only a cross-section. Variance looks easier.
2. Is a change of definition a fact being superseded, or a refinement? The
   half-life of a definition may not be the half-life of a fact.
3. Does a literature extraction replace the survey, or prepare it? A short
   survey asking immunologists which definitions they use could test what the
   extraction finds.
4. Which immuno-oncology questions from the 2024 survey draft come next, such
   as T cell differentiation markers or cytokine effects on each cell type?
5. The project has not read any sources yet. When it does, it needs a
   `references.qmd`, starting with Arbesman and Poynard.

## 6. Steps

1. Fold in the remaining thoughts from the Google Doc.
2. Check the Poynard estimate and its method.
3. Search for published reviews of B cell gating strategies and
   standardization efforts, so the extraction starts from what is already
   known.
4. Run a pilot extraction on 50 papers reporting B cell subsets and check it
   by hand.
5. Decide from the pilot whether to scale the variance measure up.
